vilayet_stats.vilayet: Bosna (1876 extent: Saray, İzvornik, Travnik, Bihke, Banaluka, Yenipazar sancakları; Hersek detached; Gusinye kazası moved to Prizren sancağı)
vilayet_stats.year: 1870 Ottoman count (Bosna Vilayet Salnamesi 1287/1870), applied to 1876
vilayet_stats.source: Male counts by sancak and millet from the 1870 salname, as given in Z. Gölen, Belleten 65/242 (2001), Tablo II. They are doubled, which reproduces Layard's 1877 figure 'Bosnie 1,242,456' = 2 x 621,228 (Köse 2019, Tablo 1). Sancak totals in persons: Saray 126,010 (56.9% Muslim), İzvornik 248,110 (52.9%), Travnik 184,802 (47.8%), Bihke 169,602 (53.8%), Banaluka 179,680 (33.9%), Yenipazar 160,496 (63.3%). The Çingene/Kıbti category (5,030 males in these sancaks) is counted as Muslim Roma. Jews (346 males, 692 persons) are excluded. Gusinye kazası (PVS 1290: 2,570 Muslim / 1,125 non-Muslim males) is subtracted from Yenipazar. The Turkish share is an estimate (officials and garrisons) with no Ottoman source behind it.

vilayet_stats.vilayet: Hersek (Hersek/Mostar sancağı; separated from Bosna as its own vilayet by 1876)
vilayet_stats.year: 1870 Ottoman count (Bosna Vilayet Salnamesi 1287), applied to 1876
vilayet_stats.source: Gölen 2001, Tablo II, Hersek column: 39,472 Muslim + 676 Çingene, 23,492 Orthodox and 18,289 Catholic males, doubled (49.0% Muslim). Gölen notes that the 1876 Bosna salname leaves Hersek out because Hersek had been organised as a separate vilayet.

vilayet_stats.vilayet: Manastır (Prizren sancağı only, in this region: Prizren, İpek, Yakova, Priştine, Gilan, Vulçıtrın ['Dehir'] and Gusinye kazas)
vilayet_stats.year: 1873/74 (Prizren Vilayeti Salnamesi 1290/1291), applied to 1876; plus Circassian muhacirs
vilayet_stats.source: Kaza male counts from PVS 1290 as tabulated in Layard 1877 (FO 881/3655) via M. Köse, Trakya Üniv. Edebiyat Fak. Dergisi 9/18 (2019), Tablo 27: sancak 93,458 Muslim / 41,099 non-Muslim males. The Priştine row of that table repeats Yakova's numbers and is replaced by the 1874 count of 258 villages with 13,435 Muslims and 5,825 Christians (Wikipedia 'Demographics of Pristina'), which matches Layard's sancak totals. Yakova is confirmed as PVS H.1290 p.112 (M. Ünlü 2017). The kaza figures are doubled, and 6,000 Circassian muhacirs (Gawrych) are added. The Prizren sancak belonged to Manastır vilayet in 1874-77 (İşkodra and Prizren vilayets merged: Osmani and Pay 2022; Wikipedia 'Manastir vilayet'). The Turkish share is an estimate for Turkish-speaking townsmen plus Mamuša and Mazgit.

vilayet_stats.vilayet: Tuna (Niş sancağı, only the İvranya/Vranya, Leskofça, Ürgüp and Kurşunlu kazas in this region)
vilayet_stats.year: c.1874-77 Ottoman figures as reported by Layard (July 1877)
vilayet_stats.source: Köse 2019, Tablo 29 (Layard, FO 881/3655), male counts doubled: Vranya 12,502 M / 30,061 NM; Leskofça 10,525 / 21,030; Ürgüp 6,207 / 4,618; Kurşunlu 5,951 / 757. Niş remained in the Tuna vilayet after 1874 (Osmani and Pay 2022, citing the Tuna salnames of 1292/1293). The Turkish share is an estimate for Turkish-speaking townsmen (cf. Hamzaoğlu 2004).

The 1863/64 census counted 196,230 inhabitants (99,889 male, 96,339 female), via Wikipedia 'Demographic history of Montenegro'. No Ottoman figure exists. The roughly 1,000 Muslims are the draft's estimate for Drobnjak.
Serbian census of 1874: 1,353,890. The okrug split is approximate. The roughly 3,500 Muslims are the draft's estimate of Muslim Roma remnants after 1867. No Ottoman figure exists.

vilayet_stats.vilayet: Avusturya-Macaristan (Dalmatia south of Zadar and the Croatian-Slavonian Military Frontier east of 15.5°E)
vilayet_stats.source: Dalmatia had 456,961 inhabitants in 1869; about 402,000 of them fall in these clusters once the Zadar district and northern islands are left out. The Slunj, Lika and 2nd Banal frontier-regiment parts (155,000) are rough estimates. No Muslims.

Küre Ansiklopedi 'Vulçıtrın': 1887 (1304) Kosova salname gives 12,145 males (9,818 Muslim, 2,327 non-Muslim). This was used to identify Layard's 'Dehir' kaza (250 villages; 6,752 Muslim / 2,571 non-Muslim males) as Vulçıtrın
Wikipedia 'Kosovo vilayet' (citing Gawrych, The Crescent and the Eagle): about 6,000 Circassian settlers in Kosovo, settled from 1864
Wikipedia 'Demographic history of Montenegro': 1863/64 census of 196,230; Serbian census of 1874 (1,353,890); Austrian census of 1869 (Dalmatia 456,961)

Retained from the draft for spatial placement only: Austro-Hungarian census of 1879 (town sizes for Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Mostar, Tuzla and Travnik; kotar patterns), Austro-Hungarian kotar patterns of 1885-1910, Bartl and consular counts for the Novi Pazar sanjak, and Natural Earth land polygons for the coordinate checks
caveats: Population totals use the Ottoman registered male count x 2, as instructed (for Bosnia this reproduces Layard's 1,242,456). McCarthy's corrected 1870 total (x 2.81, 1,746,399 for Bosna incl. Hersek and Yenipazar) is about 41% higher, with identical shares. The 1879 Austrian count (1,158,440 for Bosnia-Herzegovina without Novi Pazar, after the war) is also higher than the x 2 figure (1,074,492). So Bosnian and Herzegovinian dot densities are probably understated relative to reality, but not relative to the other regions, if those also use x 2.

The Bosnian figures date from the 1870 count, six years before 1876. They do not show the Christian refugees of the 1875-76 Herzegovina and Bosnia uprisings (well over 100,000 had fled to Austria and Montenegro) or war deaths. The map shows the settled pre-uprising pattern.

The kaza-level tables of the 1870 Bosnia salname could not be obtained. Inside each Bosnian sancak, population is allocated to clusters from approximate post-1879 district sizes, with the main towns fixed (Sarajevo 19,000 non-Jews, Banja Luka 9,500, Mostar 10,800, Tuzla 7,000, Travnik 5,800, Novi Pazar 11,000, Pljevlja 7,000). The 'kaza/district' tags in 'groups' name the 1866/1870 kazas, but the kaza totals inside Bosnia are allocations, not Ottoman kaza figures. Only the sancak totals are Ottoman.

Inside each sancak (Bosnia and Hersek) and kaza (Prizren and Niş sancaks), the draft's relative Muslim vs Christian pattern is kept. The Muslim share of each cluster gets one common odds shift (logit offset) so that the unit matches the Ottoman share. This raises the Muslim share even in largely Christian zones, for example western Herzegovina from 7% to 17% and the Banja Luka countryside from 10% to 18%. A real 1870 distribution may have concentrated the extra Muslims in the towns instead.

The Ottoman Çingene/Kıbti category in Bosnia (5,706 males in 1870) is counted entirely as Muslim Roma (muslim_other). McCarthy/Wikipedia label the category 'non-Muslim Gypsies'. If that is right, about 11,400 persons should move to christian, which would cut the Bosnian Muslim share by about 1 point.

Layard's 'Dehir' kaza (Prizren sancağı) is taken to be Vulçıtrın. Its non-Muslim male count (2,571) matches the 1887 Vulçıtrın count (2,327), but this identification is mine, not a source's. The draft's combined 'Vulçıtrın ve Mitroviçe' cluster was split: Mitroviçe was a kaza of the Yenipazar sancağı (Bosna).

Gusinye kazası was in the Yenipazar sancağı in 1866 but in the Prizren sancağı in PVS 1290. It is subtracted from the 1870 Yenipazar count on the assumption that the 1870 count included it. If it did not, Yenipazar is understated by 7,390.

Vilayet labels: the Prizren sancağı is given as 'Manastır' because the İşkodra and Prizren vilayets were merged into a Manastır vilayet in 1874-77. If the map prefers the older Prizren vilayet (1871-74, used by Layard), relabel those clusters 'Prizren'. Niş sancağı clusters are 'Tuna'. Herzegovina is 'Hersek', a separate vilayet by 1876. Preševo/Bujanovac is placed in Vranya kazası (pre-1878). Its exact 1876 kaza is uncertain.

No Ottoman source separates Turkish speakers from other Muslims in these regions. The turk values are estimates under the source policy: Turkish-speaking townsmen in Prizren (about 35% of the town's Muslims), Priştine (35%), Vulçıtrın (30%), Gilan (30%), Mitroviçe (20%), İpek (12%), Vranya (65%), Leskofça (60%) and Ürgüp (14%); officials and garrisons in Bosnian towns (1.5-5%); and the Turkish villages of Mamuša and Mazgit. Bosniaks, Albanian Muslims, Gorani, Circassians and Muslim Roma are muslim_other.

Circassians: the roughly 6,000 Circassians in Kosovo (Gawrych; a figure for the 1890s used as a proxy for the 1864-65 settlement) are added outside the registered counts. They are placed at Miloševo (2,500), around Vulçıtrın (1,500) and around Novo Brdo/Kamenica (2,000). Circassian settlers in the Niş sancağı (some existed before 1878) are not added, because no figure was found.
No soldiers are added. The large Ottoman field armies of 1876 (Herzegovina, the Drina and the Niš front) are not part of the settled population, and no sourced garrison figure was available.

Montenegro (1863/64 census), Serbia (1874 census) and the Austrian lands (1869 census) are split among clusters by approximate district weights. They are not Ottoman figures, and their shares are unchanged from the draft.

Still left to neighbouring datasets: Podgorica, Spuž, Žabljak, Bar and Ulcinj (İşkodra); Luma/Kukës; Niş kazası, Şehirköy (Pirot) and İznebol (Tran) (Tuna/Niş dataset); Üsküp sancağı (Kumanovo, Tetovo); Slavonia and Srem north of the Sava.
changes: Bosna vilayeti: Muslim shares are re-anchored by sancak to the Ottoman 1870 count (Gölen 2001, Tablo II, Çingene counted as Muslim Roma) instead of the draft's Austrian-1879-influenced aim of about 41-43%. Results: Saray 56.9%, İzvornik 52.9%, Travnik 47.8%, Bihke 53.8%, Banaluka 33.9%, Yenipazar 63.3%, Hersek 49.0%. Every cluster's odds were shifted by one common factor: Saray x1.16, İzvornik x1.39, Travnik x1.68, Bihke x1.56, Banaluka x1.97, Yenipazar x2.49, Hersek x2.70.

Population added to every cluster: Ottoman male counts x 2 (Bosna 1,068,700 + Hersek 163,858 = Layard's 1,242,456 minus Jews and Gusinye). Prizren sancağı 269,124 + 6,000 Circassians. Niş sancağı part 183,302. Montenegro 196,230; Serbia 1,353,890; Austrian lands 571,786.

Herzegovina (Hersek vilayeti, 49.0% Muslim in 1870) shows the largest shifts: Mostar town 57% to 77.5% Muslim, Foča 58% to 79%, Konjic 52% to 75%, Nikšić 40% to 64%, Gacko 38% to 62%, Nevesinje 27% to 50%, Bileća-Trebinje 20% to 40%, western Herzegovina 7% to 17% (source: Gölen 2001, 1870 salname).

Novi Pazar sancağı (63.3% Muslim in the 1870 count, Gölen 2001) is raised throughout: Novi Pazar town 75% to 88% (TDV: 1,500 Muslim vs 100 Christian households in 1857), Pljevlja town 63% to 81%, Bijelo Polje-Bihor 55% to 75%, Prijepolje-Priboj 42% to 64%, Berane 32% to 54%, Kolašin town 50% to 71%, Pešter 82% to 92%.

Bihke, İzvornik, Travnik, Saray and Banaluka sancaks are raised to match the 1870 figures. Examples: Bihać-Una 56% to 66.5%, Cazin 85% to 90%, Prijedor 50% to 61%, Zvornik 60.5% to 68%, Zenica 55% to 67%, Bugojno-Vakuf 50% to 63%, Banja Luka town 68% to 81%, Doboj-Tešanj 46% to 63%, Sarajevo city 76% to 78.6% (excluding Jews).

Prizren sancağı is rebuilt from the Prizren Vilayeti Salnamesi 1290 kaza figures (Layard/Köse Tablo 27; Ünlü 2017), with Priştine repaired from the 1874 count (13,435 Muslims / 5,825 Christians). Prizren kaza 81.1% Muslim; İpek 52.8%, which lowers the draft (İpek town 78% to 70%, Rugova-Dečani 78% to 70%, northern Metohija 38% to 28%); Yakova 88% to 82% (official); Gilan 51.9% (town 70% to 57%, Kačanik-Karadak 85% to 76%); Priştine 69.8%, which raises the draft (Kosovo plain 47% to 62%, Lab 45% to 60%, Ferizovik 55% to 69%, Priştine town 75% to 85%); Vulçıtrın ('Dehir') 72.4%; Gusinye 69.6%.

Added 6,000 Circassian muhacirs in Kosovo, absent from the 1873/74 registers (Gawrych): a new Miloševo/Mazgit cluster (2,500 Circassians plus Mazgit Turks), 1,500 at Vulçıtrın and 2,000 at Novo Brdo-Kamenica.

New clusters: Mamuşa (Turkish village, 97% turk); Kosova ovası Çerkes ve Türk köyleri (Miloševo, Mazgit); Mitroviçe kasabası, split from the draft's Vulçıtrın-Mitroviçe cluster and placed in Yenipazar sancağı (Bosna).

Turkish-speaking share raised under policy rule 6 (Turkish-speaking townsmen count as turk): Prizren town 22% to 29%, Priştine 25% to 30%, Vranya 20% to 26%, Leskofça 10% to 24.5%, Ürgüp 5% to 8%, Kurşunlu 2% to 3.5%, Vulçıtrın 12.8% (new), Mitroviçe 15.8% (new). Officials and garrisons raised modestly in Bosnian towns: Sarajevo 3.1%, Mostar 2.7%, Travnik 2.3%, Banja Luka 2.0%, Pljevlja 4.0%, Novi Pazar 4.4%, Sjenica 2.3%.

Niş sancağı kazas anchored to Layard's Ottoman male counts (Köse Tablo 29): Vranya kaza 29.4% Muslim (town 50% to 40.6%, Preševo-Bujanovac 62% to 52.7%); Leskofça 33.4% (Jablanica-Pusta Reka 72% to 79%, town 32% to 41%); Ürgüp 55% to 57.3%; Kurşunlu 88% to 88.7%. Preševo-Bujanovac moved to Vranya kazası and vilayet set to Tuna (Osmani and Pay 2022).

Administrative fields added: Bosna (Saray, İzvornik, Travnik, Bihke, Banaluka, Yenipazar), Hersek (separate vilayet by 1876, per Gölen), Manastır/Prizren sancağı (1874-77 merger), Tuna/Niş, Karadağ, Sırbistan, Avusturya-Macaristan (Dalmaçya; Hırvat-Slavon Askerî Sınırı).
